summary: The US reportedly readies Gulf allies for new Iran strikes, the Fed holds while two officials want a hike, Israel's count ends in deadlock, and Ebola in Congo passes 10,000 cases.

topics.heading: US reportedly tells Gulf states to prepare for short, intense Iran strikes after midterms
topics.summary: The Wall Street Journal reports that Washington has warned Gulf allies to brace for a brief but intense US campaign against Iran after the November 3 midterms. The White House says Trump keeps all options open; Iran warns of strikes across the region.[^3][^4]

lead.title: US warns Gulf states to brace for 'intense' Iran war after midterms

alsoReported.title: US warns Gulf of intense strikes on Iran after midterms: Report

article: According to a Wall Street Journal report summarised by other outlets, the US has told several Gulf Arab governments, through diplomatic and military channels, to prepare for a possible short but intense military campaign against Iran after the US midterm elections on November 3[^3][^4]. The report says President Trump has not made a final decision but is leaning toward a major attack[^3]. The White House would only say that Trump "keeps all options on the table"[^3].

Background: the US and Israel went to war with Iran on February 28. Iran answered with strikes on US bases and Gulf targets and closed the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane that carries a large share of the world's oil; the US then imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports[^3]. The Pentagon told Congress the war had cost $47.1 billion through October 16[^4].

Preparations are visible. The US is moving another Patriot air-defence system from Texas to Israel, restocking munitions and moving staff out of exposed bases, and another aircraft-carrier group is expected in the region next month[^3][^4]. Diplomacy has stalled: a senior Iranian official told Reuters a Qatari proposal was "unacceptable"[^4]. On Tuesday the UN nuclear watchdog said it saw no sign Iran had rebuilt its damaged nuclear sites, but it cannot inspect them or confirm where Iran's enriched uranium is[^3].

Why it matters: new strikes could again close shipping, push oil prices higher and draw in Gulf states that host US forces. My read: public warnings like this can be a real plan, a pressure tactic before talks, or both, so what happens after November 3 is the test.
topics.differences: Washington frames any strikes as keeping Iran from a nuclear weapon[^3]. Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, says any new attack would hit energy markets hard, and Iran has warned it would strike economic and military targets across the region[^3][^4]. Analysts quoted say strikes could harden Tehran's resolve rather than force concessions[^3].

topics.heading: The US Federal Reserve holds rates, but two officials vote for a hike
topics.summary: The Fed kept its key rate at 3.75% to 4% six days before the midterms. Two policymakers wanted a quarter-point increase, and markets now put the odds of a December hike near 80%.[^1][^2]

lead.title: Fed holds rates steady as a governor and president dissent together for the first time since 1992

alsoReported.title: Federal Reserve holds interest rates steady as midterm elections loom

article: The US central bank's rate-setting committee voted 10 to 2 on Wednesday to leave its benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4%[^1]. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack both preferred a quarter-point hike[^1]. It was the first time since 1992 that a governor and a regional bank president dissented on the same side[^1]. The Fed had raised rates in September, its first increase in three years[^2].

The reason is prices. US consumer prices rose 3.7% in the year to September, well above the Fed's 2% goal, partly because fuel costs have climbed during the Middle East conflict[^2]. Chair Kevin Warsh said officials want more data first, and that the "monetary medicine" seems to be starting to work, without firm conclusions[^1]. The Fed's statement upgraded its view of the economy to "expanding at a strong pace", even though September job gains were weak at 29,000[^1][^2].

Politics hangs over the decision. Inflation is a top issue in the November 3 midterms, and Deutsche Bank analysts suggested the Fed might prefer to avoid a pre-election hike[^2]. President Trump posted that rates should come down "fast"[^2]. Markets put the chance of a December increase near 80%[^2]; the next meeting is December 8 and 9[^14].

Why it matters: when the Fed raises rates, borrowing gets dearer across the world, and Canada's central bank raised its own rate on the same day. My read: the split vote shows how hard it is to fight inflation caused by an oil shock without slowing a still-growing economy.

topics.heading: Israel's near-final count leaves both blocs short as Arab-led parties hit a record
topics.summary: With about 90% of votes counted, Netanyahu's bloc has 53 seats, Eisenkot's 48 and Arab-led parties 19, a record. Netanyahu suggested high Arab turnout was an effort to steal the election; the election committee found no sign of systematic tampering.[^5][^7]

lead.title: With 90% of votes counted, Netanyahu bloc has 53 seats, Eisenkot's 48; Arab parties surge to 19

alsoReported.title: Israel election results: Netanyahu bloc at 53 seats, Eisenkot bloc at 48 as nearly all votes counted

article: By Wednesday night, about 89.8% of votes from Tuesday's election had been counted[^5]. Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc stood at 53 of 120 seats, down from 68 in the outgoing parliament, and Gadi Eisenkot's opposition bloc at 48[^5]. A government needs 61[^5]. Likud has 26 seats and Eisenkot's Yashar 21[^5].

The biggest change is among Arab-led parties: the Joint List and Ra'am together hold about 19 seats, up from 10, the most ever[^5][^6]. Whether they would join or back a government is uncertain[^6]. Yair Golan of the Democrats urges a coalition with them, while Eisenkot speaks of forming a "Zionist government"[^5][^6].

Some 430,000 to 480,000 "double-envelope" ballots, mostly from soldiers, are being counted on Thursday and could shift a seat or two[^5]. Official results are due November 4[^5]. President Isaac Herzog, who will choose who gets the first try at forming a government, has urged parties to avoid another election and negotiate "with an open mind"[^5][^7].

Why it matters: the next government will decide Israel's role in a possible new round of strikes on Iran and the next phase of the Gaza truce. My read: neither bloc can govern without a surprising partner, so weeks of bargaining, or even another vote, are realistic.
topics.differences: Netanyahu posted a video suggesting high turnout in Arab areas was part of an effort to "steal" the election[^7]. The Central Elections Committee said there were no signs of systematic tampering, and the head of the Shin Bet security service said the vote was run properly[^7]. Eisenkot says the result shows the public wants change and that Netanyahu should step down[^6].

topics.heading: Congo's Ebola outbreak passes 10,000 cases as a vaccine trial begins
topics.summary: Congo's health ministry counts 10,141 cases and nearly 5,000 deaths in the country's largest Ebola outbreak. There is no approved vaccine for this strain, and a trial has started in Bunia; Kenya has nine cases.[^12][^13]

lead.title: DR Congo: WHO urges sustained efforts as Ebola cases top 10,000

alsoReported.title: Ebola outbreak in Congo nears 10,000 confirmed cases as first vaccine trial begins

article: As of Monday, the Democratic Republic of the Congo had recorded 10,141 Ebola cases and nearly 5,000 deaths, according to its health ministry, cited by the World Health Organization (WHO)[^12]. More than 2,600 people have recovered[^12]. It is Congo's 17th Ebola outbreak and its largest, and the second-largest anywhere after West Africa's 2014-2016 epidemic[^12]. Cases have been found in eight provinces; Ituri, in the northeast, is the centre[^12][^13].

This outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a rarer kind of Ebola with no approved vaccine or specific treatment[^12]. The vaccine used in past outbreaks, Ervebo, targets a different strain, and WHO says it is not known whether it protects against this one[^13]. A trial called TUMAINI began on October 23 in Bunia to test it and other candidates[^12][^13]. Doses go first to close contacts of patients, a method called ring vaccination[^12].

The virus has crossed borders. Kenya has nine cases and two deaths, all linked to a man who travelled from Congo through Uganda; Nigeria reported a case in Abuja on October 20[^12][^13]. WHO rates the risk as very high in Congo, high for neighbours and low elsewhere, and advises against travel bans[^13].

Why it matters: eastern Congo is also living with armed conflict, hunger and displacement, which makes contact tracing hard; only about 80% of contacts are being followed, against a 95% target[^12][^13]. WHO says progress is being made but that sustained effort is essential[^12].

topics.heading: Brazil's defeated candidate Flávio Bolsonaro flies to the US as courts investigate him
topics.summary: Days after losing the October 25 runoff to President Lula by about 4.4 million votes, Flávio Bolsonaro left Brazil and landed in Miami. Brazil's Supreme Court had ordered him to hand over his passports in a corruption probe.[^8][^9]

lead.title: Defeated Brazilian candidate Flávio Bolsonaro arrives in U.S. amid investigation

alsoReported.title: Flavio Bolsonaro flees Brazil after election loss, US says will grant visa

article: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won Brazil's presidential runoff on October 25 by about 4.4 million votes over Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro[^8][^9]. Flávio Bolsonaro first refused to accept the result and talked of seeking to annul it; on Monday his Liberal Party said it accepted the outcome[^8].

Brazil's Supreme Court is investigating him in two cases involving alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion, and it ordered him to surrender his passports[^9]. He denies wrongdoing[^8]. After travelling through Argentina and Ecuador, he and his family landed in Miami on Wednesday; the US had said it would grant them visas[^9]. It is unclear whether he handed over his passports; allies say he also holds an Italian one[^9].

His Senate term ends on January 31, 2027, which also ends the special right of sitting lawmakers to be tried only by the Supreme Court[^9]. His brother Eduardo, who lives in the US, was convicted in absentia in June for illegally lobbying the Trump administration[^8].

Why it matters: Brazil is Latin America's largest democracy, and its last two elections have been followed by fights over whether losers accept the result. My read: how Washington treats a politician facing charges at home will shape US-Brazil relations in Lula's new term.
topics.differences: Trump called the election "rigged" and "strange and terrible"; Al Jazeera notes no evidence of fraud has emerged[^8][^9]. Lula called the departure shameful and said Bolsonaro should have stayed to clear his name[^8]. US Representative Joaquin Castro, a Democrat, asked whether the administration helped him leave and said losing an election is not grounds for asylum[^8].

topics.heading: Finland and Norway's leaders phone Putin, splitting Ukraine's Nordic allies
topics.summary: Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre held a 90-minute call with Vladimir Putin urging an end to the war. Denmark's and Sweden's leaders criticised the move as uncoordinated.[^10]

lead.title: Putin call pits Finland and Norway against Denmark and Sweden

alsoReported.title: Ukraine's Zelenskiy says territory recaptured, forces on the offensive

article: On Tuesday, Stubb and Støre spoke with Putin for 90 minutes at their own initiative and urged him to end the full-scale invasion and negotiate seriously[^10]. They said they spoke for their own countries, not for Europe, and briefed Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy afterward; he thanked them for their support[^10]. Euronews reports that the Kremlin's account repeated Putin's hard-line terms[^10].

The call broke an unusual Nordic consensus. Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said it was not coordinated with other Europeans and compared it with Hungarian leader Viktor Orbán's past trip to Moscow[^10]. Sweden's Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson warned that splitting Europe's voice is risky, though talks that push Russia toward peace on Ukraine's terms would be welcome[^10]. Støre argued that Europe should talk to Russia to complement Washington, which sees the war differently[^10].

On the battlefield, Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that Ukrainian forces had retaken ground, including near Kupiansk, where troops turned Russia's use of underground gas pipelines against it[^11]. Russian commanders say they are advancing along the front; neither side's claims could be independently checked[^11].

Why it matters: Europe pays a growing share of Ukraine's support, so who speaks for Europe with Moscow matters. My read: this is a quarrel over method, not goals, but it shows how hard a common European line becomes as US mediation shifts.
topics.differences: Finland and Norway present the call as complementing US diplomacy[^10]; Denmark says there is no sign Russia wants peace and that Europe must speak with one voice[^10]. Kyiv welcomed the call[^10].

question.text: Central banks in Ottawa and Washington both say energy prices are now their main inflation worry. If new strikes on Iran pushed oil higher again, trace how that could reach a Toronto family's budget. Which link in that chain is the least certain, and why?
